cases.name: card_valid
cases.why: A card with every field present decodes and re-encodes byte-identically.

cases.name: card_no_display_name
cases.why: A name is optional; omitting the key is how you decline to assert one.

cases.name: card_display_name_empty
cases.why: A present-but-empty name is a second encoding of `absent`. §18.1 admits one encoding per meaning, so this is MALFORMED rather than a name of zero length.

cases.name: card_display_name_too_long
cases.why: Names are bounded in characters, not bytes, so the bound does not silently shorten scripts needing more than one byte per character.

cases.name: card_display_name_multibyte
cases.why: Thirty-two characters of Japanese is 96 bytes. A byte bound would reject a name within the stated limit, which is why the limit counts characters.

cases.name: card_display_name_not_nfc
cases.why: A decomposed name is valid UTF-8 and non-canonical. Two encodings of one name would make H(object) depend on the sender's keyboard, so §18.1 requires NFC.

cases.name: card_inbox_key_too_long
cases.why: A record key is an address, and an address field long enough to hold a payload is a covert channel with a signature on it.

cases.name: card_inbox_key_empty
cases.why: A card whose inbox is the empty string names nothing. Absent and empty must not both mean `no inbox`.

cases.name: details_with_profile
cases.why: A whole profile: a picture, ways to be reached, and how to be referred to. None of it is in the card — the card is a QR code scanned across a counter, and a profile does not fit in one. It arrives on the record afterwards, which is also why it can change without reissuing anything.

expect.hint: avatar must be PNG, JPEG or WebP

cases.name: details_avatar_not_an_image
cases.why: Bytes handed to an image decoder on someone else's phone are one of the most reliably exploitable surfaces there is. A decoder should never have to guess what it was given.

cases.name: details_avatar_too_large
cases.why: An avatar is a thumbnail, not a file transfer, and it has to fit in the record beside everything else — a profile that does not fit is a contact nobody can reach.

cases.name: details_avatar_empty
cases.why: Present-but-empty is a second spelling of 'no picture', and omitting the key is the first.

expect.hint: not the shape of an email

cases.name: details_email_not_an_email
cases.why: These render as identity. An address with no domain is a claim about who someone is that no client checked.

expect.hint: not the shape of an email

cases.name: details_email_with_control_characters
cases.why: The reason to validate rather than escape at the screen: a field that can hold control characters is a field that renders differently in every client that draws it.

cases.name: details_phone_not_digits
cases.why: One number has a dozen spellings. Accepting all of them means two clients render it two ways and neither matches when somebody searches.

cases.name: details_signal_without_digits
cases.why: Signal's own shape is name.digits, and a username that cannot exist points at nobody.

cases.name: details_without_pronouns
cases.why: A closed set, because this is drawn next to a name on a stranger's screen and free text there is a place to put a message. Absence is not a failure state — a person with none set renders like anyone else.

cases.name: details_valid
cases.why: What each side writes into the contact inbox: who they are, where to leave things, and the keys to seal with.

cases.name: details_no_name
cases.why: The name is optional here for the same reason it is on the card.

cases.name: details_with_payto
cases.why: A contact may publish an address so they can be paid without asking first. Optional, and a real trade: a stored address is a reused address, and a reused address links every payment to that person on a public ledger.

cases.name: details_payto_empty
cases.why: Absent is how a contact declines to publish one. An empty string would be a second spelling of that.

cases.name: details_outbox_empty
cases.why: An empty outbox key would leave the other side with a contact it can never write to, reported as success.

cases.name: head_zero
cases.why: A log nobody has written to yet: the next message will be sequence 0.

cases.name: head_mid
cases.why: next_seq doubles as the count of messages ever written, which is what makes a gap detectable.

cases.name: head_with_read_watermark
cases.why: A read receipt as a head field rather than a message: the head is rewritten constantly anyway, so the watermark costs no ring slot, no prekey and no chain entry. Absent means receipts are off, which is the default — when a message was read is behavioural data and leaves the device only by opt-in.

cases.name: head_with_ring
cases.why: The ring size travels on the head so it can change: eight was sized for text, and reactions and receipts multiply message count. Readers take the ring from the head, never from a constant — the failure of a mismatch is reading the wrong slot and refusing a valid thread.

cases.name: head_ring_default_must_be_omitted
cases.why: Eight is the default and is encoded by omission — one meaning, one encoding (§18.1).

cases.name: head_ring_too_small
cases.why: A ring needs a head and at least one slot.

cases.name: ring_first
cases.why: The first message goes to subkey 1, immediately after the head.

cases.name: ring_last_slot
cases.why: Seven slots in an eight-subkey record, so sequence 6 is the last before wrapping.

cases.name: ring_wraps
cases.why: Sequence 7 wraps back to subkey 1 and overwrites sequence 0.

cases.name: ring_wraps_twice
cases.why: Wrapping is modular, not a one-off.

cases.name: chain_three_messages
cases.why: A well-formed thread: each message links to the one before and the sequence has no gaps.

cases.name: chain_first_must_link_to_nothing
cases.why: The opening message has no predecessor, so its link is thirty-two zero bytes. Anything else claims a history that does not exist.

cases.name: chain_gap_refused
cases.why: A missing message is refused rather than stored around it: a thread that silently skips one shows a conversation that did not happen.

cases.name: chain_substituted_message
cases.why: The sequence fits but the link does not, which is what a removed-and-replaced message looks like. This is the case the chain exists to catch.

cases.name: chain_replayed_message
cases.why: Re-delivering a message already accepted is a stale sequence number, not a fresh one.

cases.name: payment_request
cases.why: Asking a contact for an exact amount. It carries no authority — the payer still decides at §15.5's confirm screen.

cases.name: payment_sent
cases.why: A notice that money was sent, with a transaction to look for. Advisory: §17.5 verifies by finding the output, never by believing the note.

cases.name: payment_without_amount
cases.why: A payment screen with a blank where the number goes. Refused rather than rendered.

expect.hint: text must not carry an amount

cases.name: text_with_amount
cases.why: An amount on a text message is a number nothing will honour, which is worse than no number.

cases.name: request_with_payto
cases.why: A request names where to pay, so the payer needs nothing from a contact record that may be stale — and so the address is not stored and reused, which would link every payment to that person on a public ledger.

expect.hint: only a request names where to pay

cases.name: notice_with_payto
cases.why: Only a request names a destination. A notice doing so would be describing a payment it claims to have already made.

cases.name: payto_too_long
cases.why: An address field long enough to hold a payload is a covert channel with a signature on it.

cases.name: itemised_bill
cases.why: A bill that says what the money is for. The items plus tax add up to the amount, which is the property that makes an itemisation worth carrying — a breakdown nobody can check is a breakdown that can say anything.

cases.name: itemised_receipt
cases.why: The same lines on a notice rather than a request: a receipt for a payment already made. The vendor issues it, and it remains their claim about what was bought — the chain records the amount and never the reason.

expect.hint: items and tax must equal the amount

cases.name: items_do_not_add_up
cases.why: The one way an itemised bill is worse than none: a breakdown next to a total it disagrees with looks like a check that was performed. It was not, so the message is refused.

cases.name: items_without_tax
cases.why: Tax is optional. With none, the items alone must equal the amount.

cases.name: tax_without_items
cases.why: Tax on nothing states a split of a total the message never breaks down, so the recipient has to take it on faith. Itemisation is only worth having when it is always arithmetic.

expect.hint: empty item list; omit the key

cases.name: empty_item_list
cases.why: Present-but-empty is a second spelling of 'not itemised' and omitting the key is the first. §18.1 allows one.

cases.name: item_without_description
cases.why: A line with an amount and no words is a number on a receipt with nothing to say what it bought.

cases.name: item_description_too_long
cases.why: A description field long enough to hold a payload is a covert channel on a receipt.

cases.name: too_many_items
cases.why: A receipt is rendered on someone else's phone, so the length of the list it has to draw is not the sender's to choose without bound.

cases.name: text_with_items
cases.why: A text message has no bill to itemise.

cases.name: items_overflow_the_amount
cases.why: Two lines that sum past u64 must not wrap into a total that matches.

cases.name: itemised_receipt_from_the_payee
cases.why: A receipt is a different claim from a notice, and neither existing kind can make it: a vendor sending PAYMENT_SENT would be stating they sent money. This says 'I have your payment, and here is the breakdown it settles', and points at the transaction it acknowledges.

cases.name: receipt_without_amount
cases.why: A receipt for an unstated amount settles nothing.

expect.hint: only a request names where to pay

cases.name: receipt_with_payto
cases.why: Only a request names where to pay. A receipt doing so is asking again for money it says it already has.

cases.name: reaction_valid
cases.why: An emoji about a message, named by sequence in the recipient's log. A message like any other — sealed, chained, sequenced — because a side-channel for reactions would be a second delivery path with its own bugs.

cases.name: reaction_to_own_message
cases.why: Reacting to one's own earlier message: the target sequence is in the sender's log, flagged by presence (§18.1 — one meaning, one encoding).

cases.name: reaction_without_target
cases.why: An emoji about nothing is a text message wearing the wrong kind.

cases.name: reaction_body_too_long
cases.why: The body is the emoji. Sixteen characters holds any emoji sequence; a paragraph is a message and should be one.

cases.name: reaction_with_amount
cases.why: A reaction carries no money: an amount on an emoji is a payment nothing will match.

cases.name: target_on_a_text
cases.why: Only a reaction targets another message.

cases.name: attachment_valid
cases.why: A picture by reference: the bytes live in their own record as XChaCha-sealed chunks, and the key travels here, inside the sealed message — so the record on the network is noise to everyone but the thread.

cases.name: attachment_too_large
cases.why: One record is the unit: 32 chunks of 32 KiB is Veilid's measured 1 MiB cap, and a larger file is a different design, not a larger number.

cases.name: attachment_on_a_request
cases.why: Attachments ride ordinary messages. A bill with a file in it is two features fused at their least-tested corner.

expect.hint: only a notice or receipt carries a txid

cases.name: request_with_txid
cases.why: A notice points at the transaction it made and a receipt at the one it acknowledges. A request pointing at either is claiming the payment it is simultaneously asking for.

cases.name: attachment_partial
cases.why: All or nothing: every subset of {record, key, nonce, length, hash, mime} is a trap — fetchable but not decryptable, or decryptable but not verifiable.

cases.name: hail_valid
cases.why: A rider on a public board: a claim-once card, sixty-four bytes of destination, an offer, an expiry. The card is the only field with teeth — claiming it is what §16.9 verifies.

cases.name: hail_quote_me
cases.why: An absent fare is a real posture: name your price. Distinct from zero, which is refused below.

cases.name: hail_fare_zero
cases.why: A zero fare offer is a missing one wearing a number — two encodings of one meaning (§18.1).

expect.hint: card must be a ducat: URI

cases.name: hail_card_wrong_scheme
cases.why: The board is hostile input; a notice whose card is not a ducat: URI is bait for whatever parses the link.

cases.name: hail_dest_empty
cases.why: An empty destination says nothing and renders as something.

cases.name: hail_dest_too_long
cases.why: Sixty-four bytes of human words is the cap by construction: the place a notice can say is the cell it is pinned to. More is a channel, and the channel is the thread.

cases.name: hail_wrong_version
cases.why: A version this reader does not speak, refused rather than guessed at.

cases.name: hail_with_geocells
cases.why: An Uber-shaped hail: origin and destination as geocells no finer than ~1.2 km, so a driver reads the job — distance to the fare, length of the ride — before claiming. The cells are the only location the board ever carries.

cases.name: hail_origin_only
cases.why: Either cell may travel alone; a rider may name where they are and keep where they are going for the thread.

cases.name: hail_cell_too_precise
cases.why: Precision 7 is ~150 m — a location, not an area. The cap is what makes 'no precise location on the board' true by construction rather than by good manners.

cases.name: hail_cell_bad_alphabet
cases.why: 'a' is not in the geohash alphabet; a cell that cannot name a place is bait for whatever parses it.
